query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an in‐situ, low‐thermal‐input laser scanning strategy with substrate pre-heating during the LPBF process will enable a more controlled solidification in AlCrFeNiSi feedstock, promoting a beneficial nonequilibrium chemical short-range order that relaxes residual thermal stresses and enhances mechanical properties compared to components produced under conventional high‐thermal-load regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock possessing standard morphology and composition suitable for LPBF additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Adopt a modified laser powder bed fusion protocol using a reduced laser power density (approximately 30% lower than conventional settings) combined with an increased scanning speed (around 20% faster) and pre-heating the build substrate to 200–300°C. This regimen is intended to lower peak thermal gradients during deposition.
generation.conditions: Processing window: LPBF with reduced power and increased scanning speed; substrate temperatures between 200–300°C; use with miniature component geometries (feature sizes of 1–5 mm). Testing at room temperature through residual stress measurements and tensile mechanical testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Nonequilibrium chemical short-range order (SRO) that develops during the relatively gradual solidification enabled by the modified thermal input.
generation.mechanism: Lowering the instantaneous thermal load reduces steep thermal gradients, which in turn moderates the cooling rate. This facilitates the formation and retention of a beneficial nonequilibrium SRO state that can dissipate residual stresses and improve the microstructural integrity, leading to enhanced mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to parts made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions, components manufactured with the modified process are expected to exhibit significantly reduced residual thermal stresses and improved mechanical behavior (e.g., higher tensile strength and ductility). The process is also anticipated to simplify post-processing by reducing the need for extensive stress-relief treatments.
generation.baseline: Conventional LPBF processing of AlCrFeNiSi using high laser power without substrate pre-heating, which typically results in steep thermal gradients, higher residual stresses, and degraded mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The benefits of the intervention may be limited if the reduction in laser power impairs full densification or if the pre-heating is insufficient (e.g., below 200°C). This approach is specifically targeted to the miniature component scale; effectiveness on larger geometries remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in residual stress reduction and mechanical properties are currently uncertain, and the degree to which nonequilibrium SRO contributes to these improvements in this specific alloy requires further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components: one using the conventional high-thermal-load LPBF regime and the other using the modified low-energy protocol with substrate pre-heating. Post-build, conduct detailed residual stress measurements (via XRD and/or neutron diffraction), tensile mechanical testing, and microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM) to assess the presence and nature of SRO.
measurements: Residual stress levels (measured by X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction)
Microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM analysis for SRO indicators)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified process does not lead to statistically significant reductions in residual stresses or improvements in mechanical properties relative to the conventional process, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal differences in SRO formation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Material-agnostic machine learning approach enables high relative density in powder bed fusion products

Abstract: This study introduces a method that is applicable across various powder materials to predict process conditions that yield a product with a relative density greater than 98% by laser powder bed fusion. We develop an XGBoost model using a dataset comprising material properties of powder and process conditions, and its output, relative density, undergoes a transformation using a sigmoid function to increase accuracy. We deeply examine the relationships between input features and the target value using Shapley additive explanations. Experimental validation with stainless steel 316 L, AlSi10Mg, and Fe60Co15Ni15Cr10 medium entropy alloy powders verifies the method’s reproducibility and transferability. This research contributes to laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing by offering a universally applicable strategy to optimize process conditions. Nonequilibrium chemical short-range order in metallic alloys

Abstract: AbstractMetallic alloys are routinely subjected to nonequilibrium processes during manufacturing, such as rapid solidification and thermomechanical processing. It has been suggested in the high-entropy alloy literature that chemical short-range order (SRO) could offer a new knob to tailor materials properties. While evidence of the effect of SRO on materials properties accumulates, the state of SRO evolution during alloy manufacturing remains obscure. Here, we employ high-fidelity atomistic simulations to track SRO evolution during the solidification and thermomechanical processing of alloys. Our investigation reveals that alloy processing can lead to nonequilibrium steady-states of SRO that are different from any equilibrium state. The mechanism behind nonequilibrium SRO formation is shown to be an inherent ordering bias present in nonequilibrium events. These results demonstrate that conventional manufacturing processes provide pathways for tuning SRO that lead to a broad nonequilibrium spectrum of SRO states beyond the equilibrium design space of alloys.Subject terms: Atomistic models, Metals and alloys This
